                                         centric biases, classify each shot in isolation without leverag-
                                         ing sequential dependencies, and lack both narrative under-
                                         standing and explainability. In this paper, we present Scene-
                                         VLM, the first fine-tuned vision-language model (VLM)                                                 Scene-VLM
                                         framework for video scene segmentation. Scene-VLM jointly

                                         1. Introduction                                                        decades of research, video scene segmentation remains chal-
                                         Video scene segmentation, the task of identifying coherent             lenging as it requires understanding narrative semantics be-
                                         narrative boundaries within long-form video content, is fun-           yond visual cues, distinguishing meaningful story transitions
                                         damental to video understanding [6, 16, 17, 20, 26, 27, 31].           from superficial visual changes.
                                         Accurate scene boundary detection is crucial for organizing,               Recent state-of-the-art methods have made substantial
                                         searching, and understanding video content at scale, enabling          progress through cross-modal fusion and efficient tempo-
                                         applications such as automated structured summarization,               ral modeling. BaSSL [20] employs boundary-aware self-
                                         semantic retrieval and contextual advertising. Formally, a             supervised pretraining with pseudo-boundaries to learn tran-

                                                                                                            1
Figure 2. Proposed approach. The VLM receives a sequence of N multimodal shot representations as input. Each shot representation
consists of visual frames, dialogue, and optional metadata. Scene-VLM processes the shots within a focus window (green) using
information from a larger context window (gray), and outputs scene boundary predictions for the shots in focus in the format “Shot i:
Yes/No.” For each shot, we compute a confidence score by probing the softmax logits of the “Yes” and “No” tokens and normalize by
P (Yes)/(P (Yes) + P (No)). The model can also be aligned to generate coherent post-hoc explanations for its scene-boundary decisions.

ing [16]. Second, they all follow a mutual point-wise predic-         poral padding around a central focus window where pre-

local temporal window without leveraging causal dependen-             and future evidence. Fourth, since VLMs do not natively

2. Related Work                                                                       Vision–Language Models for Video Understanding Re-
Video Scene Segmentation Segmenting long-form videos                                  cent years have witnessed rapid progress in the utilization
into semantically coherent scenes is a long-standing prob-                            of vision–language models (VLMs) for various video under-
lem in video understanding. Early approaches cast it as                               standing tasks [11, 13, 19, 32, 33, 36]. However, video pro-
an unsupervised clustering task, grouping visually similar                            cessing remains challenging due to internal context-length
shots based on low-level descriptors [7]. While label-free,                           limitations. To mitigate this, recent works introduce hier-
such methods failed to capture narrative-level transitions                            archical representations and efficient temporal modeling to
extending beyond visual continuity. With the emergence                                extend reasoning horizons [18, 21, 33]. Among open-source
of deep learning, hand-crafted features were replaced by                              models, Qwen2.5-VL [5] demonstrates strong multimodal
CNN-based embeddings [6], and sequential models (e.g.,                                reasoning, making it a viable backbone for structured video
LSTMs) modeled temporal continuity across shots [16]. The                             understanding. Despite this emerging potential, to our knowl-
MovieNet dataset [16] enabled large-scale supervised learn-                           edge our work is the first to explore VLMs for the task of
ing and multimodal integration of subtitles, speech, and                              video scene segmentation.

   We attribute these gains to fundamental differences in
how visual information is processed. Chapter-LLaMA is
a text-only approach: it first generates text captions from
the visual signals, then processes these captions alongside
speech transcripts. Our approach instead learns directly
from raw visual frames jointly with transcripts, avoiding the              Figure 6. Scene transition explanation example. Scene-VLM +
intermediate captioning step. We believe this end-to-end                   Explain proposes a boundary in Lincoln and provides a brief ratio-
multimodal grounding enables our model to discover which                   nale grounded in visual changes, dialogue, and character presence.
visual cues are truly predictive for boundary decisions, rather            Table 9. Explainability evaluation. Comparison of explanation
than relying on caption representations that may lose salient              quality between Scene-VLM and Scene-VLM + Explain on 30
visual information.                                                        randomly sampled transitions. The explanation-supervised variant

                                                                           5. Conclusion
rendering the explanations unreliable for practical use.
                                                                           We introduced Scene-VLM, the first VLM-based framework
Alignment via Minimal Supervision. Since prompting
                                                                           for video scene segmentation. Our approach addresses key
alone proved insufficient, we turned to explicit supervision.
                                                                           limitations of prior methods through a structured multi-
However, since no large-scale annotated explanation datasets
                                                                           modal shot representation, sequential predictions based on
exist for this task, we instead set to explore whether the
                                                                           a context-focus window design and the ability to generate
model’s generation behavior could be aligned toward pro-
                                                                           natural-language rationales for boundary decisions. We fur-
ducing well-structured, grounded explanations using mini-
                                                                           ther propose a confidence prediction scheme that provides
mal targeted supervision. To test this, we curated a small set
                                                                           flexible precision-recall trade-offs, a capability typically re-
of 35 human-annotated examples, each pairing a boundary
                                                                           served for encoder-based methods. Scene-VLM achieves
with a short rationale describing the narrative transition (e.g.,
                                                                           state-of-the-art results on MovieNet and demonstrates strong
location, time, characters, dialogue topic). An additional
                                                                           generalization to BBC Planet Earth and to the video chap-
fine-tuning stage on this small set yielded an augmented
                                                                           tering task. One limitation is the structured Yes/No output
model, Scene-VLM + Explain, capable of producing co-
                                                                           format, which trades generative flexibility for reliable con-
herent, structured explanations. Fig. 6 shows this model’s
                                                                           fidence extraction; future work could explore more flexible
capability. More examples are in the Appendix.
                                                                           schemes. Looking ahead, we plan to explore reinforcement
Evaluation. To assess explanation quality, we conduct                      learning for integrating explicit reasoning into the prediction
a small-scale quantitative probe on 30 randomly sampled                    process, jointly improving both accuracy and interpretability.

               You are a vision–language model specialized in analyzing movies and segmenting them into
               scenes.
                                                                                                                         System prompt

               Analyze a sequence of shots (frames, dialogue, actor IDs) to identify scene transitions.                  Task
               Predict only on the specified subset (focus region).                                                      Context–focus scope
                                                                                                                                Legend
                                                                                                                         Multimodal inputs (XML-style)
               Full context window: shots [0-20] available for reasoning.
               Prediction target (focus): shots [5-15] only.                                                             Output
               Use context for narrative flow; emit decisions only for focus shots.


                 <shots>
                         <shot_0>
                                 [n keyframe images with shot index labels]
                                 <subtitle>[synchronized dialogue text or "[No subtitle for this shot]"]</subtitle>
                                 <actors>[character IMDb IDs and presence information]</actors>
                         </shot_0>
                         <shot_1>
                                 [n keyframe images with shot index labels]
                                 <subtitle>[dialogue content]</subtitle>
                                 <actors>[character information]</actors>

                         ...
                         <shot_20>

(scene segmentation and video chaptering).                                                   Confidence scores are essential for scene segmentation, en-

A.2.4. Chapter-LLaMA Adaptation for MovieNet                                                 from VLM outputs is non-trivial, as VLMs produce struc-
                                                                                             tured textual responses where confidence must be inferred
Adapting Chapter-LLaMA [30] to MovieNet is concep-                                           from token-level probabilities rather than dedicated classi-
tually straightforward but requires addressing a modality                                    fication heads. In this section, we compare our proposed
gap. While Chapter-LLaMA relies on rich transcripts and                                      approach against two alternative prediction schemes, which
keyframe captions, MovieNet, being cinematic, often ex-                                      differ in output format, confidence estimation capability,
hibits sparser dialogue while scene changes are predomi-                                     accuracy, and computational cost.
nantly visual. Hence, directly applying Chapter-LLaMA
to MovieNet under-detects boundaries. For a fair compari-                                    Comprehensive scheme. Our proposed scheme (see
son, we generate a caption per-shot using the authors’ VLM                                   Sec. 3.2) generates structured outputs in the format
[35] to supply the missing visual semantics, and feed these                                  shot id:<id>: Yes/No for each shot in the focus
captions to Chapter-LLaMA in the exact input format speci-                                   window, providing explicit predictions for all target shots.
fied in [30]. This preserves their pipeline while aligning the                               Confidence is then computed from the normalized token
visual signal with MovieNet’s shot structure.                                                logits as described in Eq. (3). As shown in Tab. 10, this

In this section, we present a thorough analysis of our mod-
                                                                                                                   generated rationales for scene-boundary decisions in Fig. 10
els’ computational requirements. We compare four variants,
                                                                                                                   and Fig. 11. These examples span both abrupt visual transi-
varying the number of frames per shot (1F or 3F) and model
                                                                                                                   tions (e.g., title cards) and subtler, socially driven changes
size (3B or 7B). For all models, we use a batch size of 1 to
                                                                                                                   (e.g., shifts in location, time, or conversational structure).
enable a fair comparison of memory and runtime. We do not
apply model/system optimizations such as weight/activation
quantization (e.g., 4-/8-bit) or inference engines with KV-
cache optimizations (e.g., vLLM); these could further reduce
both latency and memory in future work.
